content:
I'd like to ask for some advice. For the past few years I was formalizing math while working in industry. This year, I started my graduate studies, which has been a huge shift of pace, especially since the topic of my studies is far from formalization (dynamical systems).

What happened is that I got drown in months of exams, background reading, deadlines for research reports and paper submissions, meetings, teaching/research apprenticeships and so on.

I see that there are a lot of PhD students here and accomplished mathematicians who do work in areas other than formalization, and still somehow contribute a lot, whether in the form of reviews or formalization.

Can you please give some advice on how you are able to manage your time? How do you balance between your academic duties and your lean-related contributions?

Let me express, first of all, my admiration for taking up a PhD after years in industry, which must be very difficult. And let me share that I also often feel overwhelmed with things to do and belittled by the quality of many colleagues here; but as someone with a permanent position I can measure how privileged I am. My first suggestion is to try to avoid as much as possible comparison with other members you see on Zulip: on a one hand, some of us are in a much more comfortable position and, on the other, the temptation to consider other people's job more valuable than ours is at the same time unhealthy and often misinformed. I don't have a true practical advice, but I'm deeply convinced that it is crucial, although very hard to implement in practice, to avoid the trap of setting abstract "standards" for ourselves, and rather do what we like and for the time that we consider reasonable to devote to this activity. One of the beautiful things of Mathlib being a community is that there are other contributors helping the adventure to move on even when you feel too tired or too busy to open VSCode, yet you'll still be part of it.

I second the opinion the you are probably overrating people. What's true is that at any given time there is someone free from teaching/administration/whatever that is working a lot. But the opposite is also true, people regularly take breaks from formalization because of various reasons. Anyone should find their own balant, it's not a competition. I understand that you can say "it's easy to say so being in a comfortable position", but you should not stress too much on how productive other people are. Of course you should also think about your career, what you want to do and so on. Probably the best advice is to speak with your advisor, maybe you can find something interesting for formalization that also fits well in your thesis.

As a data point: I'm in a similar position as you, doing a PhD after spending some time in industry. I've done very little formalization that was not in some way also contributing to my PhD. While my main topic is proof assistants for education, I managed to sneak some time in to finish contributing Tutte's theorem to mathlib, so I fully second Riccardo's suggestion to discuss combining the two with your advisor.

I am not in academia (I teach a class and some seminars but that's a second gig, my first one is in industry, and I guess my third one is in OSS maintainership which is plenty of work itself). My perspective as someone with lots of interests and lots of things I'd like to learn is I find myself constantly pulled in different directions, at times doing "guilt driven development" where what gets done is what I feel most bad about neglecting previously -- I'd suggest that it's OK to constantly feel like you are not balancing things well, it's inevitable to some extent. In my case I try to take advantage of two things: sudden bursts of motivation in a direction I wanted to make progress in -- opportunistically using the morning you wake up with lots of Lean energy to make progress in an area. And second is to set medium term goals and reevaluate them, deciding on things you want to learn or get done in X months and then periodically assessing yourself against those, where it's OK to get X months later and say "eh actually I don't care about this" but maybe less OK if you say it about everything on your list constantly.

Productivity is hard!

I feel your situation. Let me emphasize that you're not alone --- you've seen so upthread also, I also feel the same (and am very privileged, e.g. full-time postdoc, where I can work on mathlib as essentially part of my job; mathlib maintainer etc.) What has helped me is realising that this will not change: I can only change where I'm spending my time. This blog post articulates a similar point, from a maintainer's perspective.

I also feel that I'm surrounded by people who know Lean much better, work longer etc. --- and this is somewhat true. But usually, that's missing part of the story --- there are things you can do well, and we tend to forget about these. I find it helpful to read this blog post by Derek Dreyer from time to time.

Regarding productivity: what helps is to be conscious of your time. Use your productive hours (and open zulip outside of them :-)); take breaks when you need to. What has helped me a lot is to value self-reflection (and reflection on your working process) as much as "working" itself... and allow yourself to fail at being productive. It's easy to say, and reality is harder than that!

Thank you for the kind words and advice! :heart:

Michael Rothgang said:

reflection on your working process

That is an interesting point, what kind of reflection, is it self-assessment?

Self-reflection: not necessarily about assessment --- but e.g. thinking about your work.
If you find it hard to start working, start thinking about why. Are you e.g. tired, distracted by personal life, bad working environment (e.g. noisy), other stress? Do you find task X difficult and that's why? etc. Free-writing has helped me a lot here.
